paragraphs.source_en: After a short arid phase around 7,000 BP the presence of pastoral groups in shelters is attested. The stratigraphical layer demonstrates a change in the subsistence pattern, dominated by domestic cattle. Di Lernia (1999) notices a continuity of settlement between the Mesolithic huntergatherers and the first herders who mainly concentrated their cattle and small stock herds in the mountains. However, pastoral ceramics and lithics are different from Mesolithic material (Smith 2005).

paragraphs.source_en: The rock shelter of Uan Muhuggiag in the Acacus, excavated by Mori (1960-1, 1990-1, 2000), is important for the occurrence of prehistoric burials. The lowest layer of occupation is attributed to the Mesolithic period dated between 7,800 and 7,400 BP. An adult individual in a crouched position was buried in the shelter; the layer immediately covering the skeleton was C14 dated between 7,823+95 and 7,550+120 BP. Another burial dated to 5,405+180 BP testifies to the existence of a cult of the dead (Barich 1998a). A child buried in a crouched position and wrapped in a leather cover tied with wicker, had a mummified body. Laboratory examinations of cutaneous remains have confirmed a darkskinned individual.

paragraphs.source_en: Uan Muhuggiag shelter is also important for the dating of a deep circular kettle carved in the basement of the shelter near a wall. It was unearthed under a layer dated at 7,438 BP, which constitutes an ante quem date for the kettle. Mori (2000) believes that the layer accumulated during the 8th millennium BP which indicates that the kettle was no longer in use and it was therefore created and used in much earlier times.

paragraphs.source_en: The Tin Hanakaten shelter in the lower part of the Tassili n'Ajjer, excavated by Aumassip in the 1970-80s, allows comparisons with the sequence from the excavated sites in the Acacus. It is a vast shelter with no Round Head paintings but some recent images. The lowest layer of the 6m deep deposit consisted of red sand with Aterian artefacts, suggesting human frequentation of the site in the Late Pleistocene. This level is separated from successive levels by aeolian sand. From the Early Holocene the shelter was continuously occupied over thousands of years. Given the presence of pottery since the earliest Holocene levels, the Francophone scholars dealing with this excavation applied the term "Neolithic" for the whole sequence (Aumassip 1980-1, 2006; Hachid 1998).
